_comment: Goal recipes for 'mammoth how'. Each step names a real command id (a unit test checks every one exists). Upper-case words in an example (VIEW_ID, DATASET_ID, ...) are ids to take from the previous step's output; {project_id} is filled from --project or the profile.

recipes.title: Refresh a dataset on a schedule (daily, weekly, hourly)
goals: keep my data up to date

steps.purpose: Check the source: only a cloud or database dataset can be refreshed. A dataset made from an uploaded file has nothing to pull.
Look for an automation that already does this. 'automation create' is not idempotent: two creates fire twice.
Create the recurring refresh: a run_data_retrieval task with an at_specific_time condition.
Read the automation back and confirm its tasks and condition.

notes: A file dataset cannot refresh itself. Upload each new file into it with: mammoth file upload ./new.csv --input '{"append_to_ds_id": DATASET_ID}'. Automating that needs a cloud connector. Run 'mammoth capabilities' for the details.

recipes.title: Add the rows of a new file to an existing dataset
goals: append a new file to a dataset
add new rows to my dataset
upload this month's data into the same dataset
add more data to an existing dataset

steps.purpose: Find the dataset to add the rows to, and its id.
Upload the new file into that dataset. The result reports the row count before and after.
Read the view back. Its pipeline re-ran over the new rows.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

recipes.title: Blend (join) two files on a shared key, such as the day
goals: combine two files on a key
merge two csv files by date

steps.purpose: Upload both files. Each one becomes a dataset with a view.
Get the view id of each dataset.
Compare the key column in both views: the same values need the same type (a TEXT date does not match a DATE).
Only if the key types differ: convert one side's key to the other's type.
steps.example: mammoth view transform convert-type VIEW_ID --input '{"conversions": [{"column": "day", "to": "DATE"}], "dataset_id": DATASET_ID}'

steps.purpose: Join the other view onto this one by the key. The result has a join_check with the match rate.
steps.example: mammoth view transform join VIEW_ID --input '{"foreign_view": OTHER_VIEW_ID, "join_type": "LEFT", "on": [{"left": "day", "right": "day"}], "dataset_id": DATASET_ID, "foreign_dataset_id": OTHER_DATASET_ID}'

steps.purpose: Read the joined rows back and check the match rate before you build on them.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

notes: Use 'view transform lookup' instead when you need one value per key and the other side repeats keys.

recipes.title: Upload a file and build a dashboard from it
goals: make a dashboard from a csv

steps.purpose: Upload the file. The result gives the dataset id and its view id.
Look at the columns and a sample before you chart them.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

steps.purpose: Generate a dashboard on the view from a plain-language intent.
steps.example: mammoth dashboard v3 generate --input '{"body": {"params": {"intent": "Revenue by region over time", "dataview_id": VIEW_ID}}}'

steps.purpose: Optional: add one more chart, from an intent or an exact figure spec.
steps.example: mammoth dashboard figure add DASHBOARD_ID --input '{"intent": "Top 10 products by revenue"}'

steps.purpose: Read the dashboard back: its figures and its link.

recipes.title: Fix an upload that is stuck (need_action, or no view)

steps.purpose: List the datasets in the project that wait for input or failed.
Read the dataset's status and status_info.
For need_action: read the detected settings (has_ambiguous_dates, delimiter, header).
Send the settings back unchanged, plus the missing decision (usually date_format US or UK).
steps.example: mammoth dataset file-settings update DATASET_ID --input '{"delimiter": ",", "has_header": true, "initial_skip_count": 0, "quotechar": "\"", "date_format": "US"}'

steps.purpose: Wait for the job the update returned.
For needs_view (an all-text file is ready but has no view): create the view. Run it only when 'view list DATASET_ID' is empty.

notes: If the status becomes error, read status_info and stop. Do not retry with guessed settings.

recipes.title: Send a view or a dashboard to Power BI
goals: publish a dashboard to power bi
use my data in power bi

steps.purpose: Push a view's rows to a Power BI dataset table. Keep the credentials in a file, not on the command line.
steps.example: mammoth view export powerbi VIEW_ID DATASET_ID --input ./powerbi.json --yes

steps.purpose: For a dashboard: check which figures Power BI can take before you export.
Export the dashboard as a Power BI file.

recipes.title: Download a view as a CSV file
goals: save the data to a local file
get a csv of my view

steps.purpose: Check the rows and the row count you are about to export.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

steps.purpose: Write the view to a local CSV file.

recipes.title: Clean a view: duplicates, blanks, column types, unwanted rows

steps.purpose: Read the view first: column_warnings lists text columns of numbers or dates, and blanks.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

steps.purpose: Fix the column types column_warnings named (a text column of numbers or dates). Convert only columns whose type is wrong.
steps.example: mammoth view transform convert-type VIEW_ID --input '{"conversions": [{"column": "amount", "to": "NUMERIC"}], "dataset_id": DATASET_ID}'

steps.purpose: Run several cleaning steps in one call (discard-duplicates, fill-missing, filter and the other ops '--help' lists).
Read the view back and compare the row count with the first read.
steps.example: mammoth view data get VIEW_ID DATASET_ID

recipes.title: Share a dashboard
goals: give someone access to a dashboard

steps.purpose: Find the dashboard id.
Share it.
Read it back.

recipes.title: Delete what you created, safely: one id at a time

steps.purpose: List what exists now and compare it with the ids you recorded before you started. Delete only ids that are not in that baseline and that the user named as temporary.
Read each id back first: it must return the name you created.
Dry-run the delete: its dependents block lists the views and dashboards that read the dataset.
Delete that one id. Never pass several ids to one delete.
Check what can still be restored.

notes: Never delete everything you own: 'owned' does not mean 'temporary'. Keep every deliverable the user asked for.
